title: Fifty Bookshops for One Book: Flipkart's First Order, 2007
dek: In October 2007 two former Amazon engineers in a Bengaluru flat got their first order, for a book they did not have, and spent two days finding it.

story.event: Starting an online bookstore from a Koramangala flat and fulfilling the first order
story.summary: In 2007 Sachin Bansal and Binny Bansal, IIT Delhi graduates who had worked as engineers at Amazon in Bengaluru, put about ₹4 lakh of their savings into Flipkart, an online bookstore run from a small Koramangala flat that aimed to beat poor service elsewhere in Indian e-commerce. Their first order, in late October 2007, was for a book they did not stock; Binny searched about 50 Bengaluru bookshops before finding a copy, and it was shipped on 31 October with a discount for the delay.
paragraphs: Late in October 2007, in a small two-bedroom flat in Koramangala, Bengaluru, Sachin Bansal and Binny Bansal received the first order on their new website. It came from a young web consultant in Mahbubnagar, then in Andhra Pradesh, who wanted John Wood's memoir Leaving Microsoft to Change the World and could not find it even in Hyderabad, 90 km away. He had found Flipkart through a comment Sachin left on his blog. The book cost about ₹500. Flipkart did not have a copy.

The Bansals, unrelated despite the surname, had met at IIT Delhi and worked as engineers at Amazon in Bengaluru. Their first idea, Sachin said in 2011, was a comparison-shopping site, but their research found Indian online shops plagued by wrong deliveries, delays and poor support. So they would run a store and compete on service, starting with books: cheap enough for a customer to risk a first order, easy to ship, and needing little capital. They pooled about ₹4 lakh of savings. Many Indian venture investors then doubted, the journalist Mihir Dalal writes, that large home-grown internet firms were possible.

The first order tested the idea at once. Binny later said they looked for the book for two days in about 50 Bengaluru bookshops and phoned others in Delhi and Mumbai. He emailed the customer to explain the delay; the customer recalled thinking, "at least this is a real company." Binny found what he said was the last copy at Sapna Book Store in Indiranagar, its pages yellowed, and had to borrow money from a roommate to pay. It was shipped on 31 October and arrived after a state holiday, with a 10 per cent discount for the wait.

Business Today later counted 20 shipments in the rest of 2007. The founders handed out Flipkart bookmarks outside Gangaram's bookshop on Church Street to people leaving with new books, persuaded two booksellers to share their stock lists, and delivered many orders themselves on bikes. Within a few months, by one account, daily orders rose from eight or ten to 30 or 40. In 2009 Accel Partners invested $1 million, and Flipkart hired its first full-time employee.

quote.text: The man who is honest and good ought to be exactly like a man who smells strong, so that the bystander as soon as he comes near him must smell whether he choose or not.
quote.source_title: Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #15877
quote.connection: Marcus wants honesty to be as plain as a strong smell, needing no announcement. Flipkart's first customer was never told the company could be trusted; he worked it out from a frank email about a book it could not yet find.

reflection: Nobody told the first customer that Flipkart was trustworthy. He worked it out from an email about a delay, and from a yellowed book that arrived anyway. The founders chose books partly so that a stranger could risk ₹500 on them; what earned the next order was how they handled the first.

You will have days when the work feels too small to matter: one reply, one sample, one apology for a delay. Those are often the moments people use to decide whether you are real. It is enough to do the small thing properly, and to say plainly when it is late.
invitation: If something you owe someone is running late today, send them a two-line note saying so and when to expect it. Then let that be enough for now.

sources.title: A bookish affair (interview with Sachin Bansal by Archana Pareek, 2011)
sources.supports: Started in 2007 with about ₹4 lakh of the founders' personal savings; the first idea of a comparison-shopping site; research showing poor customer experience, wrong deliveries, delays and weak support across Indian e-commerce; the decision to compete on service and to start with books because their low value allowed customer trials, logistics were manageable and the initial investment was small

cross_checks.claim: Flipkart's first order, in late October 2007, was for Leaving Microsoft to Change the World, which it did not stock
The founders worked from a small flat in Koramangala, Bengaluru
They started with about ₹4 lakh of their own savings
Both founders were IIT Delhi graduates who had worked at Amazon
They set out to compete on service because rivals' service was poor
The founders did their own early marketing and deliveries

research_notes: Starting money: Sachin Bansal's 2011 interview and Mihir Dalal's book both give about ₹4 lakh (₹400,000) of savings; Inc42's 2019 profile gives '$8K (INR 5.69 Lakh)', which appears to convert a dollar figure at a later exchange rate; the story uses ₹4 lakh. Early volume: Business Today (2018) says 20 shipments in 2007; Inc42 (2019) says orders rose from 8-10 a day to 30-40 'within a few months' without dating it; a Medium post's figure of 100 books in 2007 and a zero-order day on 31 December 2007 is from an unsourced blog and is not used. The story gives Business Today's 2007 figure with attribution and the daily figures as 'by one account'. The first copy: Binny's quoted account (India TV, 2015) places Sapna Book Store in Indiranagar; a search summary mentioning Koramangala could not be traced to a source and is not used. Delivery: the first order was shipped (31 October) and arrived after the Kannada Rajyotsava holiday on 1 November; claims that the founders hand-delivered it to Mahbubnagar were found only on weak sites and are not used; Inc42 reports that they delivered orders themselves by bike in Bengaluru. Business Today's 'rainy day' and India TV's account of Binny riding through rain are left out as scene detail. The first customer is named in the sources but is not named here. The India TV piece (October 2015) appears to be based on Flipkart's own Stories feature, whose original page no longer loads. YourStory's founder interviews could not be loaded by the verifier and are not cited. Flipkart Stories pages for the Koramangala house now return 'Story Not Found'. Marcus's remark is about sincerity between people; applied here by analogy.
